title_en: Apple's latest watchOS 27 beta enables Siri Recap and Live Rewind audio features
title_fa: Apple's latest watchOS 27 beta enables Siri Recap and Live Rewind audio features
excerpt_en: First revealed at the company's event in September, Apple's AI-powered Apple Watch features are finally landing in beta.
excerpt_fa: First revealed at the company's event in September, Apple's AI-powered Apple Watch features are finally landing in beta.
content_en:
Apple's latest watchOS 27 beta enables Siri Recap and Live Rewind audio features
Two of the most intriguing new Apple Watch features are here for testing.
You can now try out two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch, as long as you have one of the latest Apple wearables and you're up for installing a beta build of watchOS. The watchOS 27.3 beta includes Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which Apple revealed when it unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 back in September.
If you enable Siri Recap, you can access high-level summaries of conversations. Apple Intelligence will generate a title and key points for the conversation. The company said you can access these from the Siri app if and when you need to jog your memory.
As for Live Recap, it can convert the last 15 seconds of a conversation to text if you didn't catch or understand something. You can double-press the Digital Crown to view this snippet, ask Siri about the text or save it to view in the Siri app later. This could come in handy if you're not sure what was said in an airport announcement or a presentation, for instance.
These features are available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. The microphones on those devices can constantly pick up audio from their surroundings. There are inevitably going to be privacy concerns around an always-on microphone, which supports other Audio Intelligence features like sound recognition for things like alarms and a crying infant, and faster Shazam song detection.
Apple said these features don't record or store audio. The S11 chip that powers these Apple Watch models can process audio in isolation from the rest of the device, then delete it right away. The company claimed that its operating systems can't access the raw audio, and nor can apps, users or Apple itself.
Users can opt out of each of these features, some of which have to be manually enabled. Audio Intelligence doesn't identify or attribute speakers in conversation, Apple says. The company added that, even if an Apple Watch is set to silent, Live Rewind plays a chime when it's in use and the display shows an animation and microphone indicator. As for Siri Recap, Apple says the summaries won't show sensitive info, such as financial details.
It's worth noting that, along with an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, you'll need a compatible iPhone with Apple Intelligence enabled to use Audio Intelligence (i.e., an iPhone 16 or later but not iPhone 16e). Siri Recap and Live Rewind will initially be available only in English and not in the EU. They're also subject to daily usage limits.

title_en: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
title_fa: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
excerpt_en: Evertrue Capital announces $17M debut fund to back early stage AI and fintech.
excerpt_fa: Evertrue Capital announces $17M debut fund to back early stage AI and fintech.
content_en:
Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmellow, and robotaxi Mooves.
On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue, officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I.
“After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.”
The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.”
As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said.
However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025.
Still Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.”
Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it pour £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size.
“Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.”
Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S.
Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.”
“I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued.
She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mistusi and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.”
“I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.”

title_en: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
title_fa: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
excerpt_en: Now in beta: Apple's new Audio Intelligence features can help you remember what someone said or take notes on conversations.
excerpt_fa: Now in beta: Apple's new Audio Intelligence features can help you remember what someone said or take notes on conversations.
content_en:
Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.
However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.
Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.
With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.
Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.
When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.
These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.
The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.
Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.
Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.
This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.
At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.
This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning, too.
Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.
Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.
The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.
The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.
To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately...

title_en: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
title_fa: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
excerpt_en: Google's Dreambeans, its latest AI experiment, now supports 13 Indian languages.
excerpt_fa: Google's Dreambeans, its latest AI experiment, now supports 13 Indian languages.
content_en:
Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience.
On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older.
Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories.
Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing.
Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October.
In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries.
Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing.
That could limit Dreambeans’ appeal in India, where many people regularly switch between languages, including Hindi and English, often mixing the two in what is commonly known as Hinglish.
Dreambeans’ dependence on information from users’ Google accounts also raises questions about privacy and data access. The app uses Google’s Personal Intelligence technology to draw on connected services and personalize its AI-generated stories. Those services can contain sensitive personal information that some users may not want to share with an AI app just to receive personalized content.
Users can choose which Google services to connect to Dreambeans and disconnect them at any time, Oznur said. They can also delete their Dreambeans data from within the app. Moreover, Oznur asserted that information deleted from the underlying connected services is also removed from Dreambeans’ personalization system.
Users, Oznur said, can tell Dreambeans to avoid certain subjects, including business-related information, and the app will try to adjust its stories accordingly. She added that Dreambeans is available only to personal Gmail account holders, not enterprise users, and that generated stories are visible only to the account holder.
Dreambeans’ proactive approach also carries the risk of surfacing memories that users may find upsetting. Oznur acknowledged that Dreambeans could generate stories involving people who have died, for instance. She said users can tell the app to stop showing certain subjects, comparing the feature to controls in Google Photos that let users limit which memories appear.
Oznur told reporters that Google is exploring ways to make Dreambeans more actionable, moving beyond personalized stories and recommendations to help users act on the app’s suggestions.

title_en: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps
title_fa: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps
excerpt_en: Apple hinted at ways that it could spur revenue through third-party "opportunities" during its Monday night earnings call.
excerpt_fa: Apple hinted at ways that it could spur revenue through third-party "opportunities" during its Monday night earnings call.
content_en:
Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure. The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth.
However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear.
When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”
Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate.
Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business.
During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory.
“We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.”
Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter]. This outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from third-party licensing and the additional half percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned.”
TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for more information and will update this story if it responds.

title_en: This Chinese Android phone brand has launched a Harry Potter collab
title_fa: This Chinese Android phone brand has launched a Harry Potter collab
excerpt_en: Everything about this latest collectible Android phone is designed to evoke the popular franchise, from its magical packaging to its themed accessories.
excerpt_fa: Everything about this latest collectible Android phone is designed to evoke the popular franchise, from its magical packaging to its themed accessories.
content_en:
This Chinese Android phone brand has launched a Harry Potter collab
This collectible phone marks the smartphone manufacturer's second collaboration with Warner Bros.
Harry Potter fanatics and novelty collectors rejoice; there is now a phone that matches your passion for all things wizardry — and you can get your hands on it before HBO Max's anticipated television reboot hits streaming. Created by Chinese phone manufacturer Realme, the Realme 16 Pro Harry Potter Edition is a collectible smartphone with enough computing power to back up its unique look. Add an assortment of collectible Harry Potter accouterments, and you have a novelty item that might be worth a purchase.
For Western audiences, Realme has begun to make a name for itself as the purveyor of unique collectible phones. Last year, the firm released a limited edition Game of Thrones version of its Realme 15 Pro. The release gained rave reviews for its thematic visual elements, creative packaging and Targaryen-inspired UI designs. In its second collaboration with Warner Bros., Realme has delivered an Android phone worthy of The Boy Who Lived.
With the original run sold out within minutes of its release, ordering the unique memorabilia has been difficult. However, Realme responded to the collective interest by making a second batch available to purchase on its website. If you want some of the magic but don't have the gold Galleons to splurge on a themed Android phone, you can opt for the company's Harry Potter-inspired earbuds, the Realme Buds T500 Pro.
A spellbinding collab
Everything about Realme's latest collectible Android phone is designed to evoke the popular franchise. Coming in "Magic Brown," the phone's classic argyle design and leathery finish is sure to make some buyers want to board the Hogwarts Express. A golden Hogwarts crest stands proudly in its center, touting what the company claims is "the world's first quadra light sensing color-changing technology." When exposed to UV light, the crest transforms into a spellbinding spectrum of colors, with each house crest lighting up in its respective colors. Featuring golden accents around its cameras and siding, the ultra-thin 8.47mm-wide phone sports a laser-engraved "Welcome To Hogwarts" banner across its frame.
The phone's packaging is just as charming. Buyers of the Harry Potter Realme 16 pro will receive a small leather suitcase emblazoned with a golden Hogwarts crest. Inside, you can find your acceptance letter, book list, train ticket, character postcards, four house crest bookmarks, and a crest pin to unlock your "Hogwarts Hidden Surprise," the aforementioned wizard-themed Realme Buds T500 Pro earbuds. The unlocked phone also comes with a Harry Potter-inspired protective case, charger, USB data cable, SIM ejector tool, and a helpful guide.
Much like its Game of Thrones predecessor, Realme has customized its user interface to mimic Warner Bros. ' films. When you boot up your new collectible phone, you will find a wallpaper of Hogwarts' iconic castle, a boot animation mimicking the film's title card, and a custom Harry Potter fingerprint effect. The Chinese manufacturer also added Harry Potter redesigns for 30 of its native applications, complete with custom logos and fonts to create a more immersive fan experience.
Inside the Hogwarts phone
Realme's phone is an adequate Android smartphone that justifies its midrange price tag. With 12GB of RAM and 254 GB of ROM, the novelty phone should be capable enough for most daily users.
Despite its razor-thin size, the Realme 16 Pro's 7,000mAH titan battery is surprisingly strong. With up to 22 hours of streaming, you can watch all eight Harry Potter films without reaching for a charger. Charged with an 80W USB-C cable, the battery includes Bypass Charging to reduce overheating.
Fans will appreciate the phone's FullFocal Portrait Lens Kit, which includes a 200MP full-pixel LumaColor Camera, a 112-degree wide camera and a 50MP selfie camera. The camera suite also includes a Samsung HP5 1/1.56-inch sensor for higher resolution and brightness, plus Super Optical Image Stabilization tech to reduce blurriness and shakiness. It can also capture 4K video at up to 30fps.
The phone's 144Hz AMOLED display can reach a peak brightness of 6,500 nits. With a 94% screen-to-body ratio, you can watch HDR10+ content on a 6.78-inch display. With a pixel ratio of 1272x2772, the phone's screen has more raw pixels than an iPhone 18.
Unfortunately, Realme's processor isn't as magical as its exterior. Powered by a Taiwanese MediaTek Dimensity 7300 Max 5G chipset, the phone is unlikely to wow you with class-leading compute. Add a midrange graphics unit like the ARM Mali-G615 GPU, and you have a decent processor capable of meeting most daily needs, including gaming at 120 FPS.
Overall, the Harry Potter edition of Realme's 16 Pro is a capable midrange phone with good battery life, a strong trio of cameras, and a decent processor. The special edition device is retailing for around $657 on Realme's website.

title_en: Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them
title_fa: Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them
excerpt_en: A Kyiv startup’s pocket-sized, 10-ounce receiver lets Ukrainian troops watch the video feeds of Russian drones, though Russian moves toward digital video and AI-guided drones that emit no signals could make the victory short-lived.
excerpt_fa: A Kyiv startup’s pocket-sized, 10-ounce receiver lets Ukrainian troops watch the video feeds of Russian drones, though Russian moves toward digital video and AI-guided drones that emit no signals could make the victory short-lived.
content_en:
Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen.
Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits.
According to Defense News, the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds.
It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal.
Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals.

title_en: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
title_fa: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
excerpt_en: Y Combinator Garry Tan has jokingly admitted that he's suffered from "cyber psychosis” and barely sleeps sometimes because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast, The Builders, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
excerpt_fa: Y Combinator Garry Tan has jokingly admitted that he's suffered from "cyber psychosis” and barely sleeps sometimes because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast, The Builders, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
content_en:
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.
On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.
“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.
He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”
As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.
For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”
Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.
“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”
But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

title_en: Is it actually safe to charge your iPhone at airport USB ports?
title_fa: Is it actually safe to charge your iPhone at airport USB ports?
excerpt_en: Using a random USB charger can be unsafe, even though the risk is minimal. Thankfully, you have ways to protect your devices.
excerpt_fa: Using a random USB charger can be unsafe, even though the risk is minimal. Thankfully, you have ways to protect your devices.
content_en:
Is it actually safe to charge your iPhone at airport USB ports?
While the risk is overblown, it exists. But it's easy to protect yourself.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
The short answer is that it's reasonably safe to use public USB charging stations at airports and elsewhere. While US agencies, including the FBI and Transportation Security Administration (TSA), have warned against doing so, security researchers say the threat is overblown.
"When you're at an airport do not plug your phone directly into a USB port," the TSA warned in a March 2025 Facebook post. "Bring your TSA-compliant power brick or battery pack and plug in there." The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) published its own warning about these "juice-jacking" (also called "port-jacking") attacks, but subsequently withdrew it once tech experts disputed the extent of the threat. In 2019, the Los Angeles County district attorney warned about the threat, but subsequently confirmed it had no cases on its books.
Security pros say that while the threat is real in principle because proof-of-concept demonstrations exist, there are no credible reports of any successful attacks taking place. That doesn't mean the threat is non-existent — it's one among a multitude of potential attacks. To keep it that way, you should always take steps to secure your device.
What is the risk of juice-jacking?
The risk of juice-jacking is inherent to the USB standard, which carries both data and power along a single cable on separate internal pins. Proof-of-concept tests have shown attackers could potentially modify public USB charging points, making them connect to the data pins in your USB cable to install malware or steal data.
One proof of concept at Black Hat USA in 2013 saw researchers from Georgia Tech present a malicious charger prototype named Mactans. They illustrated how the charger could install malware on a connected iPhone running iOS 6.
OS developers pay attention to emerging risks. For example, in the months following the Mactans revelation, Apple hardened iOS with the "Trust This Computer?" prompt you now see when you connect to a new device that wants to establish a data connection. No matter how you connect your phone, if a prompt appears asking you to "Trust" it, always tap "Don't Trust" unless you intend to share data with that device.
What you can do to prevent juice-jacking
If you want zero risk, it's best to not use public USB chargers at all, as the TSA indicated. Carrying a rechargeable USB battery pack, or using your own power brick and cable with a standard wall socket, are both safer options. Where available, using "Secure" charge points that block data transfer entirely can also work.
When you do have to use public USB ports, you can greatly reduce the risk with inexpensive USB data blockers, like those from JSAUX. These small dongles block data transfers but permit energy passthrough, enabling safer use of unknown USB connections. The drawback is that USB-A blockers prevent fast charging standards because chargers use the data connection to manage high voltage electrical flow. Your device will still get charged, but it will take longer. This isn't an issue with modern USB-C blockers.
As always when traveling (and when at home), standard security advice remains the same: avoid using public Wi-Fi for sensitive information, install the latest software updates and enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) for important accounts. If you must use a public USB charging point, decline any trust prompt and consider a data blocker for added protection.

title_en: Hinge tests a cheaper plan as users become more fed up paying for dating apps
title_fa: Hinge tests a cheaper plan as users become more fed up paying for dating apps
excerpt_en: At a time when people are increasingly tired of dating apps, Hinge is testing a cheaper subscription plan.
excerpt_fa: At a time when people are increasingly tired of dating apps, Hinge is testing a cheaper subscription plan.
content_en:
Hinge is testing a cheaper subscription plan as its parent company Match Group looks for new ways to get users to pay for dating apps at a time when people are increasingly tired of subscriptions and, in some cases, dating apps altogether.
During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call on Monday, Match Group said the new Hinge tier will include features such as additional filters and custom location boundaries, giving users more control over who they see and where they meet people.
“It’s designed for women in particular, but also for price-sensitive users,” said Steve Bailey, chief financial officer of Match Group. “Remember that Hinge is one of the highest-priced products we have. The revenue per payer, for example, at Hinge is almost twice that of Tinder, around $30. It also has one of the lower payer penetrations. Its payer penetration is only slightly more than half that of Tinder.”
Match Group didn’t share how much the new subscription will cost. TechCrunch has reached out to the company for more details.
The move comes as dating apps continue to struggle to convince people to pay for services they’re growing tired of using. Between subscription fatigue, endless swiping, and frustration with the overall dating experience, users are increasingly questioning whether premium dating features are worth the money.
Interestingly, Hinge is making this move despite being one of Match Group’s strongest performers. The app had a much better quarter than Tinder, with global monthly active users growing 12% year over year, direct revenue increasing 19%, and paying users rising 23% to 2.3 million. The app generated $221 million in direct revenue and had 2.3 million paid subscribers as of the end of the quarter. Direct revenue is money earned from subscriptions and in-app purchases.
By comparison, Tinder brought in $480 million in direct revenue but experienced a slight 2% decline year-over-year, although it has 8.9 million paid users, a 4% decline from a year earlier.
The lower-priced subscription could help Hinge build on that momentum by converting more users into paying customers without requiring them to spend as much upfront.
The move also marks a shift in Hinge’s subscription strategy. In 2023, the company experimented with a more expensive tier aimed at users willing to pay extra for features designed to help them get more out of the app. Now, it’s testing whether a more affordable option could appeal to a broader audience.
Still, cheaper subscriptions alone are unlikely to solve the bigger problem facing dating apps: user fatigue. Match Group says it’s seeing some signs of improvement, partly thanks to efforts to make its platforms feel less like traditional dating apps.
Recent initiatives include Group Hangouts and Events, which offer users alternative ways to connect beyond the usual one-on-one matching experience. Match Group plans to ramp up those efforts in the fourth quarter.
Another initiative on the horizon is real-time adaptive recommendations, which the company plans to begin testing in the fourth quarter. Announced during its CEO Connection presentation in September, the feature will allow Tinder to respond to user actions within seconds rather than hours, with the goal of making recommendations more relevant and personalized.

title_en: The reason why some iPhone calls don't have a decline option, and others do
title_fa: The reason why some iPhone calls don't have a decline option, and others do
excerpt_en: Sometimes your iPhone lets you decline a call and sometimes it doesn't. Here's why that happens, and a few easy ways to handle the calls you'd rather skip.
excerpt_fa: Sometimes your iPhone lets you decline a call and sometimes it doesn't. Here's why that happens, and a few easy ways to handle the calls you'd rather skip.
content_en:
The reason why some iPhone calls don't have a decline option, and others do
Your iPhone's incoming call screen isn't as mysterious as it seems.
At some point, everyone's been burned by their iPhone going off in the worst possible place. When you see there's no option to decline the call, it's a mad scramble to press every side button or sling the phone through a wall at the speed of sound. But you've seen the on-screen option to decline calls before, so what gives? Fair warning: it's a really simple, forehead-slapping answer. When your iPhone is locked, incoming calls display the "slide to answer" control. When your iPhone is unlocked, you get the option to answer or decline the call.
Depending on your Incoming Calls setting, Accept and Decline buttons appear in a compact banner or across the entire screen, but both options remain. No, you didn't disable anything by accident. This is simply how the iPhone operates by default, right out of the box. On the bright side, it's not set in stone; you can make adjustments via Settings.
You don't need an on-screen button to decline or silence a call, however. You can press the side button twice quickly to decline and send the caller straight to voicemail. Or, you can press either volume button to silence the ring without declining the call. You can do this whether the iPhone screen is locked or not.
How to respond to an iPhone call without answering it
The person calling will probably know their call was just rejected if you hit the side button twice the moment your iPhone starts ringing. The practical effect is pretty obvious. Fortunately, rejecting a phone call doesn't have to come off as rude, because you can let the caller know why you rejected it. An iPhone's incoming call interface includes a Message option that lets you send a text instead of answering. There are a few useful prepared options, as well as a custom alternative if you prefer.
If the incoming call pops up as a banner while you're busy, tap the banner to reveal more options, then select Message. Go with a prepared reply or quickly fire off a text by choosing Custom. Now you can provide some context to the caller and explain why they're being sent straight to voicemail.
You can also change the prepared replies well in advance. Open Settings > Apps > Phone > Respond with Text, then select a response and edit it accordingly. For instance, "I'm working right now" and "Please text me; I'm busy" both speak volumes in a few short words. It's a nifty little feature and only takes a few minutes to set up.
How to reject unwanted calls on an iPhone
Despite the 1991 Telephone Consumer Protection Act, telemarketers, spam and robocalls are something we all deal with on a regular basis. According to the Federal Trade Commission, there were more than 2.6 million Do Not Call complaints in fiscal year 2025. Some callers are more persistent than others, and even if you block one number, they'll call back from another slightly different number. But it's worth the effort to block them all. Find the number you just rejected in Recents, tap it (or the Info button in Classic view), scroll to the bottom of the screen, select Block Caller and confirm.
You can use a broader setting to screen unknown callers as well. Go to Settings > Apps > Phone > Screen Unknown Callers (iOS 26 and later). From here, you can select Never, Ask Reason for Calling or Silence. Consider the middle option, just in case the unknown number is someone you know and the call is important.
But if you choose Silence, every unknown call will go straight to voicemail without ringing. Just remember that life comes at you fast, and that unknown number may be someone you recently met or someone who lost their phone and really needs to contact you. Convenience always comes with a caveat or two.

title_en: Why it's important to never plug power strips into each other
title_fa: Why it's important to never plug power strips into each other
excerpt_en: Power strips are lifesavers when you don't have enough outlets to power all of your electronics and some also offer protection from power surges.
excerpt_fa: Power strips are lifesavers when you don't have enough outlets to power all of your electronics and some also offer protection from power surges.
content_en:
Why it's important to never plug power strips into each other
Your power strip needs a wall outlet and not another power strip.
There are so many work-from-home devices nowadays that running a home office or a gaming area easily turns into a charging and power-consumption nightmare of tangled cords, ports and outlets. The idea of stringing power strips together by plugging one into the other (daisy-chaining) is a convenient, understandable solution. More outlets and ports mean more organization and power for each device. Unfortunately, it's not the greatest of ideas, especially if tripped breakers and house fires aren't on your to-do list.
The first problem is that adding sockets doesn't increase electrical capacity. Everything connected to the second strip draws electricity through the first strip's plug and internal components. The first strip is now carrying the combined load of the devices plugged into the second strip. The second problem is each strip's maximum rating, typically expressed in amps. If a second power strip is plugged into the first and the first is maxed out, the second strip could be the straw that breaks the proverbial camel's back, drawing too much and overheating the first strip.
Pushing too much current through the internal wiring and components of the first power strip generates "resistive heating." Given enough time, it can melt the casing and wire insulation, possibly igniting nearby materials. In the aforementioned home office scenario, flammable materials are abundantly present in most cases.
What to do when one power strip is no longer enough?
What to do when one power strip isn't enough depends on what you need. Do you need more sockets? Ports? More reach or more electrical capacity? Where low-power electronics are concerned, a single power strip that's more generous with its number of outlets is your best bet. Just make sure that the total load remains within the power strip's rating. A strip with 8 outlets doesn't necessarily supply more power than a strip with only 4 outlets. It's a separate consideration you have to be wary of.
If distance is the issue, find a strip with a longer cord. Don't reach for an extension cord as a matter of convenience. NFPA explicitly advises folks to avoid that arrangement, since extension cords have their own ratings and too many devices plugged in at once can exceed those ratings. Of course, you can do the math based on the cord's rating, the strip and everything plugged into it, but most people aren't aware of the limitations.
If a single strip is tripping the breaker, adding a new one and dispersing the devices won't solve the problem. In fact, treat it as a warning that requires your immediate attention. Never use a strip with damaged casings, scorch marks or loose connections. It's not something you can wrap in half a roll of electrical tape and call it a day.
What should you never plug into a power strip?
As it happens, plugging a power strip into a power strip isn't the only thing you should avoid. High-power appliances can easily overload a power strip if it's not rated to handle it. Space heaters are a common one in this regard. They draw a fairly substantial amount of current and should only be plugged into a proper wall outlet. Microwaves and refrigerators are other prime examples.
For the safest route, use ordinary power strips with ordinary devices like PCs and printers, or to charge your phone. Also, six outlets doesn't mean it needs six devices plugged into it at once. Check the devices and match them against the power strip's ratings. They may seem like it, but power strips are not all-purpose devices for whatever needs power at the moment.
Lastly, a surge protector doesn't change the dynamics here. Surge protection deals with sudden voltage spikes but, like power strips, it won't magically conjure more energy capacity. Basic safety guidance for surge protectors also advises against daisy-chaining. The potential consequences warrant a repeat: check the surge protector's or power strip's rating and what you're plugging into it. If it's not enough, simply use another outlet or purchase a separate power strip and use another wall socket to run it.

title_en: Apple says it’s ‘hard to predict’ when iPhone Duo constraints will improve
title_fa: Apple says it’s ‘hard to predict’ when iPhone Duo constraints will improve
excerpt_en: Apple says iPhone Duo production is ramping up, but it still can't say when supply will catch up with demand as shipping delays stretch into next year.
excerpt_fa: Apple says iPhone Duo production is ramping up, but it still can't say when supply will catch up with demand as shipping delays stretch into next year.
content_en:
Apple Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan acknowledged the shipping delays plaguing the new iPhone Duo during the company’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, but offered little clarity on when customers can expect relief.
The delays were just one point of concern during an earnings call filled with questions about the rising costs of memory chips, driven by soaring demand from the AI industry.
“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan said.
Customers who didn’t wait in line at an Apple Store or immediately jump on preorders are now seeing ship times stretch into next year. Meanwhile, Verizon has been apologizing to its customers for the delays by offering gift cards.
In an October report from Financial Times, Apple described demand for the Duo as “nothing short of extraordinary,” after the device sold out on the company’s website within hours of going on sale, pushing delivery dates into next year.
The prolonged shipping delays are notable given Apple’s reputation for its highly efficient supply chain. But the company is hardly alone in facing supply pressures. Soaring demand for memory chips from the AI industry has driven up component costs for hardware makers across the board, threatening to push device prices even higher.
Apple, too, has raised prices on a number of products, Khan noted on the call, adding that those decisions were made “reluctantly.”
In another sign of the company’s efforts to meet demand for the Duo, Apple said it’s “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer for supplying materials for the new foldable device.
“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Apple CEO John Ternus said during his opening remarks.

title_en: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
title_fa: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
excerpt_en: The one-year-old startup is now valued at $300 million.
excerpt_fa: The one-year-old startup is now valued at $300 million.
content_en:
Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training.
Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).
Trajectory, a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks.
The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.
Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch.
The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time.
With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper.
Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available.
The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said.
Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes.
Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. Other companies going after this market include Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect, a platform that helps companies build and train their own AI agents.
Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team. He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix.
Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers.

title_en: Apple’s inventory surges 154% as memory chip costs climb
title_fa: Apple’s inventory surges 154% as memory chip costs climb
excerpt_en: Apple says unprecedented memory chip costs will continue to rise, raising questions about future device prices as its inventory climbs to $14.5 billion.
excerpt_fa: Apple says unprecedented memory chip costs will continue to rise, raising questions about future device prices as its inventory climbs to $14.5 billion.
content_en:
Apple’s stockpiling of inventory, particularly computer memory, continued in its fiscal fourth quarter, according to earnings reported Monday. The company reported that its inventory increased significantly in the quarter, growing from $11.09 billion in Q3 to $14.54 billion in Q4, a jump of 31.1%. Year-over-year, inventory grew 154.3% from $5.72 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025.
Apple’s forecast of a 45% to 46% gross margin in the December quarter was largely attributed to the impact of higher memory costs. The company reported a gross margin of 47.9% for the September quarter.

The company also blamed supply constraints for weak iPad sales in the quarter. The iPad was one of the only product segments that didn’t grow, even as iPhone and Mac sales beat estimates. iPad revenue was $6.2 billion, below analysts’ expectations of $6.7 billion. The figure was also down 10% from the prior year.

title_en: How to use your phone's camera to translate anything
title_fa: How to use your phone's camera to translate anything
excerpt_en: With the aid of a quick picture, you can use your phone's camera to translate pretty much any text while you're traveling across the globe.
excerpt_fa: With the aid of a quick picture, you can use your phone's camera to translate pretty much any text while you're traveling across the globe.
content_en:
How to use your phone's camera to translate anything
Our phones have the ability to make sense of other languages (and it requires minimal effort on our part).
If you're a frequent traveler, you may frequently encounter signage or other text in foreign languages. That's all well and good if you have enough knowledge to piece together a translation, but if you can't even understand the alphabet in question, you're faced with a much bigger challenge.
The good news is that your phone's camera can recognize and translate just about any text in seconds, even if the language uses an entirely different script. While a translation app may seem like the obvious choice for this task, it's actually not always your best bet. Depending on the languages involved and the context, you may sometimes need more than one tool. Luckily, your phone's camera is all you need to translate pretty much anything in the real world.
The simplest way to translate text with your phone's camera
For over a decade now, the Google Translate app has offered a dedicated camera mode. Simply install the app from the Google Play Store on Android or the App Store on iOS, open it, and tap the Camera icon located at the bottom of your screen. This will open up a viewfinder, allowing you to point your phone's camera at anything in the real world.
You can select any two of Google Translate's hundreds of languages for the translation. The default "Detect language" option in the source field is handy if you've come across a language you cannot identify. The app translates text in real time, so you don't even need to capture an image. You may also want to download frequently-used languages within Google Translate. This allows you to translate text offline — handy if you're preparing for an upcoming trip.
You can also use Google Lens on Android, which many phones include out of the box these days. This eliminates the need for a dedicated translation app. On Google Pixel phones, Lens is available as a shortcut within the search bar on the home screen. Otherwise, you can find it as an icon in the app drawer. Recent iOS versions also have a translation feature baked into the camera app through the Live Text feature. To access it, open the Camera app on your iPhone and point the device at any text you come across. You should see a yellow frame appear around the text and a grid icon towards the bottom of the viewfinder. Tap this icon and select Translate.
AI apps can translate text too, and often do a better job
While Google Translate has served me well, it can fall short of expectations. While traveling in Vietnam, for instance, I found that the app struggled to identify diacritics in printed text through my phone's camera. This was a major problem because a word can have two completely different meanings depending on whether the letters have the correct diacritics. In my experience, another area where Google Translate stumbles is restaurant menus. Menus often use informal shorthand or a single word, meaning the app may lack enough context for an accurate translation.
The solution I've found is to translate via an AI app. These apps often cannot translate in real time and require an internet connection, but I've found that the output quality is far and away better than Google Translate. Modern AI models understand context, so sending a picture of a menu will typically yield food-related translations. Even if your image is blurry or difficult to read, the AI model often understands the intended meaning based on the surrounding text instead of replying with gibberish.
You can use any AI app such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude. You'll need to upload a picture of the text you need translated and type a short instruction, such as "Translate to English," before sending the message. The AI will reply with the translated text, but cannot overlay the translation over your image as Google Translate does. The other downside to this method is that it's much more expensive — ChatGPT's free tier limits you to a few image uploads every day, and even then, processing can take a few seconds. Still, I often use it as a last resort whenever traditional translation methods fail me.

title_en: Apple is ‘not able to predict’ when it’ll have enough iPhone Duos to go around
title_fa: Apple is ‘not able to predict’ when it’ll have enough iPhone Duos to go around
excerpt_en: Apple CEO John Ternus doesn't have a timeline for when iPhone Duo supply constraints could lift. During an interview with Reuters, Ternus said the company is "working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this ​point, we're not able to predict when...
excerpt_fa: Apple CEO John Ternus doesn't have a timeline for when iPhone Duo supply constraints could lift. During an interview with Reuters, Ternus said the company is "working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this ​point, we're not able to predict when...
content_en:
Apple CEO John Ternus doesn’t have a timeline for when iPhone Duo supply constraints could lift. During an interview with Reuters, Ternus said the company is “working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we’re not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”
Apple is ‘not able to predict’ when it’ll have enough iPhone Duos to go around
John Ternus says Apple is seeing ‘unprecedented’ memory pricing.
John Ternus says Apple is seeing ‘unprecedented’ memory pricing.
Apple launched its first foldable last month for $1,999, featuring a 5.4 outer display and 7.6-inch inner screen. Preorders for the iPhone Duo quickly sold out, with some shipments expected to arrive in 2027. Apple also made a limited number of iPhone Duo models available in-store at launch.
In his interview with Reuters, Ternus also addressed reports about cracked screens, saying “a very small percentage” of iPhone Duos were returned for this issue, and that Apple is replacing them.
The company has contended with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs for months now. This resulted in price increases across its product lineup, along with higher iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starting prices. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” Ternus said during Apple’s Q4 2026 earnings call on Monday. Ternus added that the company expects to see “even higher memory costs” during Apple’s December quarter but notes that this is “partly offset” by recent price increases.
Even without a standard iPhone 18 model, Apple reported record-breaking iPhone revenue at $57.58 billion during its fourth quarter.

title_en: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
title_fa: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
excerpt_en: RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return.
excerpt_fa: RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return.
content_en:
While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1/A on Monday (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print.
The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI).
RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals.
To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more.
Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’”
When the term RSI became popular earlier this year, many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove.
But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below):
In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred.
For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.
However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.”
Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category.
Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grown leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly.

title_en: Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone
title_fa: Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone
excerpt_en: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales - despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh. In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last...
excerpt_fa: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales - despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh. In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last...
content_en:
Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh. In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.
Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone
iPhone revenue jumped 17 percent with Pro-only models during this year’s refresh.
iPhone revenue jumped 17 percent with Pro-only models during this year’s refresh.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model. The company raised prices across its older models at the same time. Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products. Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027. “We saw higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, and that was partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on non-memory components,” Apple CEO John Ternus said during an interview with CNBC.
Apple reported a 12 percent increase in revenue overall, ballooning to $114.5 billion. Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks. It made a big push into the smart home space with its first smart home display and a series of video doorbells, security cameras, and door locks, made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

title_en: Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027
title_fa: Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027
excerpt_en: Meta is planning to release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, the company announced today. The last OS update for those devices is planned to be v213, and after that, Meta will continue to ship security patches and critical bug fixes...
excerpt_fa: Meta is planning to release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, the company announced today. The last OS update for those devices is planned to be v213, and after that, Meta will continue to ship security patches and critical bug fixes...
content_en:
Meta is planning to release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, the company announced today. The last OS update for those devices is planned to be v213, and after that, Meta will continue to ship security patches and critical bug fixes through the end of 2027. Apps that support the Quest 2 or Quest Pro can also be submitted through December 2027, Meta says.
Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027
The Quest 2 and Pro were discontinued in 2024, and next year, Meta will stop releasing OS updates for the VR headsets.
The Quest 2 and Pro were discontinued in 2024, and next year, Meta will stop releasing OS updates for the VR headsets.
Meta is calling the Quest 3 and 3S “now the baseline for Meta VR gamers.” The company is announcing this shift ahead of the planned release of its new VR Glasses, which are set to launch sometime in spring 2027.
“Quest 2 and Quest Pro laid the foundation for this platform, and millions of people still play on them,” Meta says. “Quest 3 and Quest 3S give your apps more performance headroom and mixed reality built in, and apps built for them carry forward to Meta VR Glasses, which run on the same OS and SDKs.”
Meta launched the Quest 2 in 2020 and the Quest Pro in 2022. It discontinued both products in 2024.

title_en: How long could HDDs and SSDs remain expensive?
title_fa: How long could HDDs and SSDs remain expensive?
excerpt_en: Thanks to shortages of microchips and other computer components, we've been experiencing high prices for years.
excerpt_fa: Thanks to shortages of microchips and other computer components, we've been experiencing high prices for years.
content_en:
How long could HDDs and SSDs remain expensive?
There might be relief in sight.
If you've spent a considerable amount of time building and maintaining custom PCs, you've likely seen it all. You've seen fads come and go, and you've seen emerging technology become permanent fixtures. Recently, however, we've all seen the disastrous end results of what is now being referred to as RAMageddon.
The chip shortage that we're dealing with today often feels reminiscent of the one from 2020, when both video game consoles and prebuilt PCs became frustratingly difficult to obtain, though they each have different root causes. While RAM, processors and even video cards are experiencing some astonishingly high prices, two PC components that have found themselves slightly shielded from the massive price hikes are hard drives and solid-state drives.
Though they are still being heavily impacted, the industry appears to be heading toward some form of relief. It may just take a bit of time to get to the finish line.
The current state of HDDs and SSDs
The current market for HDDs and SSDs is an interesting one. Regardless of whether you're buying an enthusiast drive with upwards of 20 terabytes of storage or something on the lower end, you're going to be paying significantly higher prices due to the chip shortage.
In the long run, however, deciding on the actual purchase of any kind of storage is a complicated one. Traditional mechanical hard drives have been pushed aside for years in favor of SSDs, but they do still have their uses in today's market. Though they are not ideal for gaming and often seem to move at a snail's pace compared to even baseline-level SSDs, they do function quite well for mass storage of photos, videos and documents.
They also tend to be exceptionally well built, as companies have been making them for decades. Standard HDDs have a tendency to last for quite a long time, and to that end, the comparative price between them and more advanced SSDs is nothing but a good thing. Since SSDs use flash memory, which is undergoing its own shortage, a lot of NVMe and SATA SSDs are being hit somewhat harder.
A wave of relief in 2027, but the endgame won't be until 2030
The year 2027 has been earmarked as the first wave of relief from the higher prices. Though it's often described as just a slight decrease, any bit of money saved is worth it in the long run. Ultimately, the full weight of RAMageddon's first crushing blow looks like it will start winding down, and the far-reaching effects are something that we've dealt with for a while.
Heading into 2027, industry analysts have been quite clear that things will see a trend toward lower prices, but the global lows of pre-COVID times are likely a permanent thing of the past. Indeed, it's possible that many of us may not even notice the slight dip in prices, as something that is expensive being just slightly less expensive may not feel as warm and fuzzy as one may hope.
The general consensus about when HDD and SSD prices may drop isn't a very reassuring one. 2027 may see some subtle drops, but if you're looking to build a PC, or even upgrade a drive in your current setup, it's probably wise to wait until at least the end of 2027 or beyond. Most reports have indicated that 2029 or 2030 will be when prices start to see a sharper, more noticeable drop.
