title_fa: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
excerpt_en: Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it's "terrible" to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI's impact on...
excerpt_fa: Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it's "terrible" to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI's impact on...
content_en:
Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math, Altman said:
Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.
As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”
Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now.

title_en: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
title_fa: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
excerpt_en: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI...
excerpt_fa: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI...
content_en:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.
The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers.
The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers.
The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s robots.txt file, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.
The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default.
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token. Meta communications head Andy Stone also signaled support for the new setting, but doesn’t say whether the company will honor it. “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” Stone says. “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.”
Microsoft says it will offer granular controls that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or AI grounding, the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations. Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences. Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their content appears in AI search features or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.
While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year. OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.”
Update, October 30th: Added a comment from Meta.

title_en: Meta settles another social media addiction case just before trial
title_fa: Meta settles another social media addiction case just before trial
excerpt_en: Snap is now the only defendant in the case.
excerpt_fa: Snap is now the only defendant in the case.
content_en:
Meta settles another social media addiction case just before trial
Snap is now the only defendant in the case.
Meta has reached a settlement in another social media addiction lawsuit in a move that will allow it to avoid a trial that was set to kick off next month. Snap is now the only defendant in the case, which is one of several closely watched lawsuits against social media platforms.
The lawsuit was brought by an 18-year-old woman from Mississippi known as K.D.B who, according to Reuters, has "described staying awake for hours scrolling social media, losing focus in class and engaging in self-harm using methods shown in social media videos." Jury selection kicked off earlier this week in Los Angeles.
On Friday, K.D.B's lawyer announced that she had reached a settlement with Meta after previously settling with TikTok and YouTube. "We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," attorney Emily Jeffcott said in a statement.
Terms of the settlement weren't disclosed and Meta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Now, Snap is the only remaining defendant in the case. CEO Evan Spiegel is expected to testify in the trial that could last several weeks. If he does take the stand, it will be the first time the Snap founder has appeared in a social media addiction trial. Snap previously settled in another high-profile case involving similar claims. A jury later ruled against Meta and YouTube in the trial and the two were ordered to pay $6 million in damages.
In a statement, a Snap spokesperson didn't comment on Meta's settlement, but said the lawsuit "fundamentally misrepresent(s)" how Snapchat works. "From the beginning, Snapchat was built differently from traditional social media: it opens to a camera, not a feed, not a ranking of what other people post or other social comparison metrics," the spokesperson said. "We have built safeguards into the platform, introduced safety tools and educational resources, and we believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs' experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed."
Meta and Snap have both faced a flood of lawsuits over alleged safety lapses and social media addiction. Snap also recently settled a long-running lawsuit over its "speed filter," which is alleged to have played a role in several high-speed car crashes involving teens.

title_en: Bluesky now has a dedicated 'moderation inbox'
title_fa: Bluesky now has a dedicated 'moderation inbox'
excerpt_en: The beta feature makes it easier to stay on top of reports and account strikes.
excerpt_fa: The beta feature makes it easier to stay on top of reports and account strikes.
content_en:
Bluesky now has a dedicated 'moderation inbox'
The beta feature makes it easier to stay on top of reports and account strikes.
Bluesky is rolling out a new feature today that will allow users to track the platform's various moderation actions in one place. The new "moderation inbox" is available in beta through the Bluesky app, and collects reports you've filed about other users and posts, actions taken against your account and your overall standing on the platform.
You can enable the moderation inbox by turning on beta features in the Bluesky app's Settings menu, and then finding the inbox under the Moderation tools menu. Bluesky says the inbox will start empty, even if you've already received a strike, but will fill up as you file reports about posts and Bluesky takes action against your account or applies labels to your posts. The inbox also lets you appeal most of Bluesky's decisions directly through the app, though suspensions still have to be handled at the login screen.
Bluesky says the goal for the feature is to make it easier to communicate with users. The company has previously shared moderation decisions over email, which it says made it difficult to reach people using Bluesky on independent servers, and often meant that when it did email, it was only for serious decisions. The inbox allows anyone who uses the Bluesky app to be contacted with a notification and lets the company share each step of the moderation process without cluttering anyone's email inbox.
Bluesky has earned a reputation for offering robust blocking tools that make it easier for users to moderate their own feeds, but the company's own approach to moderation has drawn criticism. In 2025, The Guardian reported that Bluesky's automated spam system regularly deactivated the accounts of Palestinians crowdfunding for supplies on the platform, which critics said treated people like bots. Users similarly took issue with the company's moderation of posts dealing with the assassination of Charlie Kirk. Clearer in-app notices and appeals might have softened some of the backlash.
Alongside the moderation inbox, Bluesky's latest update also adds an optional widget users can place on their home screen that displays trending topics.

title_en: AI law firm Crosby bids on disintegrating, famed firm Weil Gotshal
title_fa: AI law firm Crosby bids on disintegrating, famed firm Weil Gotshal
excerpt_en: Like a real-life episode of "Suits," the demise of famed white-shoe Wall Street law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges has been the talk of the legal industry. And now an AI firm has entered the picture.
excerpt_fa: Like a real-life episode of "Suits," the demise of famed white-shoe Wall Street law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges has been the talk of the legal industry. And now an AI firm has entered the picture.
content_en:
Like a real-life episode of “Suits,” the demise of famed white-shoe Wall Street law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges has been the talk of the legal industry this week. And now Silicon Valley has entered the picture.
Two-year-old AI-first law firm Crosby has put in a bid to buy some of the assets of Weil Gotshal, including its trademark, its brand, and some unspecified internal data, TechCrunch has confirmed. Separately, it is also working to hire some of the firm’s 1,200 lawyers. The Information was first to report this offer.
The once-prestigious Weil Gotshal confirmed to the New York Times this week that it was preparing to vote on dissolution in the coming days. The wind-down is happening after the firm’s presumed leadership heir apparent turned down the role, a number of its top-producing lawyers left, and a hoped-for merger with its rival, Willkie Farr & Gallagher, was shelved, the Times reported.
Meanwhile, Crosby’s founders believe they are the future of law firms. Rather than selling their internally developed AI tech to existing firms like Harvey or Legora, Crosby is an actual law firm. It uses its AI to provide legal services at, the startup promises, a speed never before possible.
The startup has raised about $85 million, including a $60 million Series B round in March led by Lux and Index, with participation from its seed-lead Sequoia, Elad Gil, 01 Advisors, and Bain Capital Ventures. Crosby came out of stealth mode in 2025 armed with $5.8 million in seed money.
While no one has pointed to the rise of legal AI as a contributing factor to Weil Gotshal’s downfall, AI may be key to the legal industry’s future. Terms of the bid weren’t disclosed and there’s no guarantee that Crosby will prevail. But if it does, Weil Gotshal’s legacy could somehow rise from the ashes, transformed by an AI-first firm.

Two-year-old AI-first law firm Crosby has put in a bid to buy some of the assets of Weil Gotshal, including its trademark, its brand, and some unspecified internal data, TechCrunch has confirmed. Separately, it is also working to hire some of the firm’s 1,200 lawyers. The Information was first to report this offer.
The once-prestigious Weil Gotshal confirmed to the New York Times this week that it was preparing to vote on dissolution in the coming days. The wind-down is happening after the firm’s presumed leadership heir apparent turned down the role, a number of its top-producing lawyers left, and a hoped-for merger with its rival, Willkie Farr & Gallagher, was shelved, the Times reported.
Meanwhile, Crosby’s founders believe they are the future of law firms. Rather than selling their internally developed AI tech to existing firms like Harvey or Legora, Crosby is an actual law firm. It uses its AI to provide legal services at, the startup promises, a speed never before possible.
The startup has raised about $85 million, including a $60 million Series B round in March led by Lux and Index, with participation from its seed-lead Sequoia, Elad Gil, 01 Advisors, and Bain Capital Ventures. Crosby came out of stealth mode in 2025 armed with $5.8 million in seed money.
While no one has pointed to the rise of legal AI as a contributing factor to Weil Gotshal’s downfall, AI may be key to the legal industry’s future. Terms of the bid weren’t disclosed and there’s no guarantee that Crosby will prevail. But if it does, Weil Gotshal’s legacy could somehow rise from the ashes, transformed by an AI-first firm.

title_en: Everything you need to know about Googlebooks
title_fa: Everything you need to know about Googlebooks
excerpt_en: Despite good initial hardware, the Googlebook OS still needs a lot of work.
excerpt_fa: Despite good initial hardware, the Googlebook OS still needs a lot of work.
content_en:
Everything you need to know about Googlebooks
Despite good initial hardware, the Googlebook OS still needs a lot of work.
It's somehow been almost two and a half years since Google said it would migrate its laptop operating system from ChromeOS to Android, and the results of that effort are finally out in the wild. Google and its hardware partners officially launched Googlebooks earlier this month with the promise of tight integration between your Android phone and this new, Android-powered laptop OS, plenty of AI-powered tricks and premium hardware.
As someone who has used and tested ChromeOS extensively over the last decade (!), I've been wondering what exactly would differentiate the Googlebook OS from ChromeOS. Google's initial Googlebook introduction in May didn't give us a ton of information, but a big demo event and several weeks of testing has given me a better idea of what the company is shooting for. And after my time with Googlebooks, I can say that while there might be benefits internally for Google (as well as third-party developers) to move from ChromeOS to Android, the upside isn't fully there for potential buyers yet — particularly when you consider how expensive Googlebooks are.
A quick word on hardware
This isn't a formal review of one Googlebook but rather an evaluation of the operating system Google is pushing. But it's worth talking quickly about the Googlebook hardware launching alongside the OS. Most of my testing was done on the $1,299 ASUS Googlebook 14, an extremely thin and light laptop that weighs in at only 2.2 pounds. It features an OLED touchscreen with Corning's Gorilla Matte glass, which significantly cuts down on reflections. From a specs standpoint, it runs on an Intel Core Ultra 5 chip with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. It's a really lovely laptop, as it should be at that price point. I also did some testing on the Acer Googlebook 14 and HP's Googlebook 14, the latter of which runs on the Snapdragon X Elite X1E-80-100 processor. Performance felt similar whether using the Intel or Qualcomm models, though I anecdotally feel like battery life was better and fans kicked in less frequently on the HP.
The Googlebook introduction positioned these new devices as premium computers, and indeed they are priced to match that claim. The least expensive Googlebook out there, Acer's Googlebook 14, starts at $899 — and that's the only Googlebook under $1,000. And while various manufacturers (including Google itself) have released premium, expensive Chromebooks over the years, Acer's $899 Googlebook is more expensive than nearly all the Chromebooks on the market.
Eventually, Googlebooks will fully replace ChromeOS, so I expect a future wave of devices will focus on affordable options. But for now, Googlebooks are strictly a premium experience with a price to match, and that'll be a big part of my evaluation of the OS. It's always been easier to forgive any limitations you might find on a Chromebook when they were priced at $400 or $500, but it's a lot harder when we're in the $1,000 range where you can get a more versatile Mac or Windows PC.
Out of the box
Setting up a Chromebook isn't hard — you generally just log in with your Google account. But Google is emphasizing the ties between your Android phone and Googlebook right from the first step, where you're prompted to set up with an Android device or even an iPhone or iPad. When I selected Android device, a notification popped up on my Pixel 11 asking me if I wanted to use it to set up my Googlebook. The laptop, meanwhile, had a QR code for scanning at the ready.
After scanning that code, my Googlebook connected to Wi-Fi and then asked me if I wanted to use the Google account from my phone. After that, I just confirmed my name and profile picture, set a login password and added a fingerprint to unlock the device. Finally, it asked if I wanted to copy apps and data from my phone, which didn't take long at all. I don't think all that much was shared, but there's a customize option for those who want to be specific about what moves over. Finally, I got a quick tour of some of the Googlebook's Gemini-powered features like Magic Pointer, the Quick Insert key and using voice chat with Gemini Live.
I was also prompted to set up the connection between my phone and the laptop so I could do things like see notifications and files from my phone on my Googlebook. That involved giving some services permission on both devices, but it didn't take long nor was it too complicated for the average user.
Once everything was set up, I was greeted with a desktop that, unsurprisingly, was quite similar to ChromeOS. There's a taskbar along the bottom with shortcuts to apps like Chrome, Gemini, Gmail and a handful of other Google services, and there are also some shortcuts on the desktop that are organized in folders for productivity (apps like Docs and Drive), media (voice recorder, PDF viewer and camera) and messaging (Gmail, Messages and Meet). Wisely, the Googlebook also booted up with an in-depth walkthrough for things like accessing quick settings, changing your wallpaper and screensaver, finding files, managing your windows and all the initial things you'll want to be able to do on a laptop. I definitely appreciated the tutorial — not that the system would have been unfriendly to use without it, but having some guidance for tips and tricks in a brand-new OS is smart.
While it's easy to mistake the Googlebook UI for ChromeOS, there are a few subtle differences here. The taskbar is exclusively for apps; the time, date, notifications and quick access to system settings are in a thin strip at the top of the screen now. I'm hit or miss on that change. On the one hand, the ChromeOS taskbar feels pretty cluttered now, but on the other I don't love giving up vertical pixels to the info bar at the top of the screen.

excerpt_en: Google's AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku...
excerpt_fa: Google's AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku...
content_en:
Google’s AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space:
Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
The Project Suncatcher satellite generated a haiku about being in space.
The Project Suncatcher satellite generated a haiku about being in space.
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google launched the satellite into orbit earlier this month.
“Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit,” Google says. “Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.”

title_en: Satlyt takes another step toward turning satellites into space data centers
title_fa: Satlyt takes another step toward turning satellites into space data centers
excerpt_en: Satlyt ran a successful test this month bringing it closer to turning spacecraft, starting with satellites, into virtual data centers.
excerpt_fa: Satlyt ran a successful test this month bringing it closer to turning spacecraft, starting with satellites, into virtual data centers.
content_en:
Naturally, Rama Afullo’s first reaction was, “Let’s GOOOO,” he said. His company, Satlyt, is building software to turn existing satellites into data processing networks, similar to the orbital data center concept. And he just took another step closer to that.
After 13 months of work, the company had a successful test earlier this month. Working with the University of Houston on a NASA-funded research project, the test showed how the startup’s software can spread out tasks among computers while in orbit based on communication and available compute.
He said the goal is to create software that connects to multiple satellites to share computing assignments. Users of the system “will only need to define permissions, priorities, and operating limits,” while the software will make decisions within those limits, Afullo told TechCrunch. Its software is already on three satellites in orbit and the first step to that vision was this test. While the test used NASA-funded research, the agency has not yet selected it for any particular mission or chosen it to deploy its technology.
Afullo said NASA missions face the same constraints that Satlyt hopes to address — “limited computing resources, intermittent communication, and the need to get useful information back to people.”
In this test, the company created a simulated network with four computers, four users, and eight services. The software then assessed how to assign and run tasks on those computers, accounting for compute and communication availability. One physical computer aboard a spacecraft ran the experiment, evaluating a simulated network of four computing hosts, then returned the results to Earth. The test proved that Satlyt’s software can generate plans on hardware in orbit, but more testing will be done to see how those computers transfer information amongst each other in practice when multiple physical computers are used.
“The finding is a trade-off,” he said. One approach worked best, though it required more computing power than the others.
Still, Satlyt which was in the top five of TechCrunch Disrupt Battlefield this year, calls this a win. “It’s a building block toward satellites sharing computing work,” he said.
NASA already has a technology network designed to move data through space even when communication links face delays. It started using this tech earlier this year and has already tested it on aircraft.
Afullo, who previously worked at Google and SpaceX, founded Satlyt in 2024 to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers. Its software helps operators run AI and other applications onboard, processing data closer to where it is collected and reducing dependence on downlinks, where satellites send data back to Earth, and ground-based analysis.
For example, if a spacecraft sees a wildfire on Earth, such software can help it transmit relevant information much faster. “The goal is to get useful answers to people sooner and make better use of limited communication windows,” he said. “This experiment tested one planning component of that broader capability.”
Satlyt said it still needs to test its own software under various workloads, hardware, and connectivity conditions. They also found an issue in how their software was time-referencing delays, Afullo said — it was stamping it as arrival time (the time it arrived) rather than elapsed delay (how long it took to arrive), which is a different metric.
It doesn’t mean the experiment failed, however. “The software development, onboard execution, and return of outputs succeeded,” he said.
But Afullo said much work remains. “We also need usable communication links, permission from participating operators, secure transfers, resource scheduling, and recovery when a connection of computers becomes unavailable.” Satlyt is also researching applications beyond low Earth orbit, including supporting 4K video streaming from the Moon through its NASA-funded work.
“Our next technical steps are broader validation and integration, followed by demonstrations of computing work shared across separate spacecraft,” he said. “Longer term, we want developers to build applications for space without having to rebuild the infrastructure for every mission. That’s what virtual AI data centers in space mean to us.”
This piece was updated.

title_en: Zest’s new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text
title_fa: Zest’s new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text
excerpt_en: Can't agree on where to eat? Zest's AI concierge can combine everyone's tastes, put restaurant options to a vote, and make the reservation.
excerpt_fa: Can't agree on where to eat? Zest's AI concierge can combine everyone's tastes, put restaurant options to a vote, and make the reservation.
content_en:
Zest, the restaurant discovery app that launched earlier this year, is already thinking about a future where mobile apps are no longer the primary interface. On Thursday, the startup introduced a new feature: a personal AI-powered “restaurant concierge” that lives in your text messages, similar to other popular AI agents like Instinct or Poke.
The launch reflects a broader shift in how startups are thinking about AI, as conversational AI agents take on tasks that had previously required users to launch stand-alone mobile apps. For Zest, that means bringing its restaurant recommendations into texts, then allowing users to immediately take the next step of booking a table.
“The agent is the product now,” explains Zest founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall. “You text it, and it answers from your own history and your friends’. It doesn’t need weeks of conversation to learn you because it starts from where you’ve actually been,” he said.
Originally founded in November 2024, with $1.8 million in pre-seed backing from Alexis Ohanian at 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, the app’s unique feature is that it links up with users’ credit cards to track where they’re actually eating out to get a sense of their tastes and interests. With this data on hand, Zest can make tailored suggestions of what places you might like to try next, whether that’s in your own city or suggestions of places to try when you’re traveling.
The credit card data used by Zest’s app is imported via the financial services company Plaid, which is used by banks and other fintech and budgeting apps. Zest says it focuses only on those transactions in the food and drink categories when making its personalized map and lists.
The startup’s latest idea is to tackle the same problem — where should I go to eat? — from a new angle. It will now make its suggestions from inside a text message thread and can turn to AI to do things like check availability and make the reservation for you through connected services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms.
To work, users will text the Zest concierge at (212) 470-6067. What’s even better is that Zest can be dropped into a group chat, where it can blend everyone’s tastes to find places the whole group will love. Here, it can also settle indecision with an in-thread voting feature and then can book a table for the group without leaving the conversation.
Users can ask Zest for recommendations based on a number of factors, like cuisine, craving, occasion, dietary restrictions, or neighborhood, and can ask questions about the restaurants, like how busy the place may be, or whether it offers Wi-Fi, and more. Plus, you can ask Zest to send you the menu to help you make a decision.
In TechCrunch’s tests, the AI worked fairly well, offering a list of suggestions for new places matched to our tastes that also fit particular conditions, like time of day, party size, location, and other factors. While finding an open table is something other apps have offered for years, there’s a convenience factor in being able to just text back and forth about the various options and have it tell you the available booking times.
The company began testing the concierge last month, but decided to hold the launch until it could add the booking capabilities; over time, the startup is considering moving Zest beyond restaurants to offer recommendations for businesses, shopping, and more.
By shifting to texts, Zest hopes the company can scale beyond its initial thousands of users and generate revenue.
“Booking and ordering are the first revenue lines. Zest books your table through OpenTable or Resy today, with food ordering coming, and there are transactions there to participate in,” said Gomez-Hall. “The reason that gets interesting is that Zest learns your taste faster than a general assistant does, because it starts from where you’ve actually been instead of asking you questions. That’s worth something well beyond dinner,” he added.

content_en:
Starbucks could eventually show you a personalized digital menu when you pull up to the drive-thru. During an earnings call on Thursday, Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said the company is going to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless,” as spotted earlier by More Perfect Union.
Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
The coffee chain aims to ‘recognize’ customers as they arrive.
The coffee chain aims to ‘recognize’ customers as they arrive.
It sounds similar to the technology that Taco Bell is experimenting with, which could change the layout, content, and visuals on a digital menu board “on a car-by-car basis.” McDonald’s also recently showed off an AI-powered feature it’s piloting at a handful of drive-thrus, allowing its “ArchIQ” chatbot to identify repeat customers and let them order their “usual.”
Starting in 2027, Starbucks will also begin testing background AI models at the drive-thru to help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” according to Niccol. The company also plans to integrate AI into the Starbucks app’s search and discovery features, and may allow “conversational and agentic” ordering in the future.
Starbucks has already started allowing customers to place orders through ChatGPT, and also rolled out an AI-powered Green Dot Assist that employees can use to ask questions about things like recipes and service standards.
It’s still not clear how soon we can expect to see personalized digital menu boards at Starbucks, but Niccol says it’s still “early,” adding that “we’ll test, learn, and scale what works.”

content_en:
The iPhone has more screens! The MacBook has a touchscreen! The HomeView does CarPlay apps! For the first time in a long time, Apple is in a period of unabashed gadget experimentation, and while the final results aren’t always perfect, it’s fun to watch the most successful product maker try some new things again. Even when, in this case, “trying” amounts to just slapping a touch panel on a lovely new MacBook Pro — just to see if you might use it.
The delightfully messy state of Apple gadgets
On The Vergecast: MacBooks, Duos, Instagram’s AI problem, and Brendan Carr’s war on the weather.
On The Vergecast: MacBooks, Duos, Instagram’s AI problem, and Brendan Carr’s war on the weather.
On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate the merits of a touchscreen laptop, Nilay explains why he is absolutely positively going to buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and David asks, as always, could this have been an iPad?
After that, the hosts discuss Instagram’s foray into long-form content, and Adam Mosseri’s increasingly complicated relationship with AI content. Instagram is at once extraordinarily powerful and under serious threat, and Mosseri’s going to have a hard time making it all work. Finally, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, news about Anthropic’s IPO and Anduril’s laptops, and much more.

title_en: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
title_fa: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
excerpt_en: During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company's still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions. But the company faces a crucial test later this year,...
excerpt_fa: During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company's still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions. But the company faces a crucial test later this year,...
content_en:
During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
RJ Scaringe spent nearly half of Rivian’s earnings call hyping self-driving tech. But taking on Tesla’s FSD with custom chips and pricey lidar is an enormous gamble while the mass-market R2 is still scaling up.
RJ Scaringe spent nearly half of Rivian’s earnings call hyping self-driving tech. But taking on Tesla’s FSD with custom chips and pricey lidar is an enormous gamble while the mass-market R2 is still scaling up.
But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call.
Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.)
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”
— Derek MulveyBut it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse.
Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued:
So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us.
But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.”
Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin.
Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers.
The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.
To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

title_en: Vizio’s discounted Mini LED TV lets you skip the sign-ups and smarts
title_fa: Vizio’s discounted Mini LED TV lets you skip the sign-ups and smarts
excerpt_en: Modern smart TVs let you skip the streaming device, which is convenient, but they also come with their own issues, including privacy concerns and frequent updates. The Vizio Mini LED Quantum TV lets you cut out the rigamarole and just get straight to the HDMI ports. And right...
excerpt_fa: Modern smart TVs let you skip the streaming device, which is convenient, but they also come with their own issues, including privacy concerns and frequent updates. The Vizio Mini LED Quantum TV lets you cut out the rigamarole and just get straight to the HDMI ports. And right...
content_en:
Modern smart TVs let you skip the streaming device, which is convenient, but they also come with their own issues, including privacy concerns and frequent updates. The Vizio Mini LED Quantum TV lets you cut out the rigamarole and just get straight to the HDMI ports. And right now, it’s discounted at Walmart, with the 65-inch model going for $358 ($40 off) and the 85-inch model going for $698 ($100 off).
Vizio’s discounted Mini LED TV lets you skip the sign-ups and smarts
If you prefer a dedicated streaming device or console, you can save some cash on an otherwise-modern television.
If you prefer a dedicated streaming device or console, you can save some cash on an otherwise-modern television.
Although Vizio’s Mini LED TV comes loaded with Vizio OS, you can bypass the TV’s host of agreements during setup. By pushing past the manufacturer’s warnings about “missing out” on smart TV features, you can disable the built-in operating system, letting you use your own streaming device like a Roku or Apple TV 4K without worrying about what data Vizio and Walmart might be collecting.
As for specs, the TV features quantum dots for full, vivid color and high brightness (our testing showed it can reach 936 nits when calibrated thanks to its mini-LED panel). There are some compromises, though, which is expected given the low price point. The IPS panel doesn’t have the best black levels, as you might see on more expensive sets, and there’s a touch of motion blur during faster scenes, which may also hurt its appeal for gamers. It also has three HDMI ports, but they’re only 2.0, although the screen only supports up to 4K at 60Hz, so it’s not detrimental to the experience.

title_en: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
title_fa: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
excerpt_en: The first TPU in space is running a Google DeepMind Gemma 4 model and writing cheesy poetry.
excerpt_fa: The first TPU in space is running a Google DeepMind Gemma 4 model and writing cheesy poetry.
content_en:
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.
After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.
A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.
The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.
Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.
If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.
Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.
Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.
In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles.
Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth.
Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

title_en: New tvOS 27.2 features to try for an upgraded Apple TV experience
title_fa: New tvOS 27.2 features to try for an upgraded Apple TV experience
excerpt_en: Apple's tvOS 27.2 update isn't a particularly transformative one, but it still introduces a handful of new features that are worth checking out.
excerpt_fa: Apple's tvOS 27.2 update isn't a particularly transformative one, but it still introduces a handful of new features that are worth checking out.
content_en:
New tvOS 27.2 features to try for an upgraded Apple TV experience
No major changes here, but tvOS 27.2's new features are welcome additions all the same.
Apple recently released iOS 27.2 to the public alongside macOS 27.2 and tvOS 27.2. For Apple TV, this was the first update since tvOS 27 debuted in September, because Apple skipped version 27.1 entirely. Unlike iOS, tvOS updates don't usually come with release notes, but a support document on Apple's website outlines exactly what changed in tvOS 27.2. There aren't any major changes this time, but you'll still find a few new features to try out. From new screen saver options to FaceTime improvements, here's everything new coming to your Apple TV with the latest tvOS.
Screen savers with more variety and FaceTime upgrades
Apple TV probably has some of the best screensavers of any streaming box, and while they aren't its biggest selling point, they're definitely a pleasure to look at. Until now, you had to choose a single category, but tvOS 27.2 changes that.
The update adds a new "Shuffle" option that cycles through Aerials, Memories, Portraits and Snoopy. Now, every time your TV enters screen saver mode, it will show you something different. You can now use your iPhone to choose specific photos for your screensaver without sharing your entire photo library with your Apple TV. This helps a lot if you share your home with others and don't want all your personal photos suddenly appearing on the big screen.
Apple has also updated the FaceTime experience, starting with FaceTime links. These make it easier to join a call directly from your Apple TV, although the call still uses your iPhone as a webcam via the Continuity Camera feature. FaceTime now also lets you add third-party sign language interpreters and live captioning services to your calls. This feature is also available for iPhone, iPad and Mac with their respective updates.
Find My for the Siri Remote and sign language in the player
The new Apple TV 4K comes with a new Siri Remote that improves Find My support and even includes a speaker so you can easily locate it. Although you will need a new device — or at least a new remote — to get this feature, tvOS 27.2 still brings a small improvement to previous Apple TV models. The remote now appears in the Find My app, so you no longer need to open the TV Remote from your iPhone's Control Center to locate it. It's a small change, but it makes the experience more consistent.
Select movies and shows on the Apple TV app now support ASL and BSL, and you can turn them on using the player controls or in Settings. Speaking of the TV app, it finally gained profile support on iPhone and iPad with iOS 27.2, and they now sync with your Apple TV. Apple even added new characters to the profile selection screen. If you share your Apple TV with others or have kids at home, the profile feature is definitely worth trying out. Another small detail in tvOS 27.2 is the new black-and-white Apple Music icon, which matches the one added in iOS 27.2 as part of the platform's new identity.
If you haven't updated your Apple TV yet, you can do so by opening the Settings app, going to System and selecting Software Update. The update is free and available for the second-generation Apple TV 4K (released in 2021) and later models. Note that some new features, such as setting up a surround sound system with two pairs of the new HomePod mini 2 (or HomePod 2nd generation), are exclusive to the new Apple TV 4K with the A19 chip introduced earlier this month.

title_en: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is ‘a great opportunity to go deceive people’
title_fa: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is ‘a great opportunity to go deceive people’
excerpt_en: The cautionary Theranos tale takes on a new significance in the AI era, when companies that have never turned a profit are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations.
excerpt_fa: The cautionary Theranos tale takes on a new significance in the AI era, when companies that have never turned a profit are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations.
content_en:
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary capturing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes’ final weeks before prison, is sparking national conversation as it becomes one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time. The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, intentionally refuses to characterize Holmes as a master manipulator or victim, instead highlighting her uncanny, almost hypnotic knack for making people pity her, even when they’re well aware of her crimes.
Tyler Shultz didn’t need to see “You Can See Everything” to make up his mind about Holmes. Shultz, whose first job out of college was at Theranos, was a key whistleblower who exposed the company’s dangerously inaccurate blood testing devices, which made their way into Walgreens stores and delivered faulty results to real patients. (Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion despite its technology never actually working — the company only used its own machines for a fraction of tests, instead outsourcing others to third-party equipment.)
There is little reason to keep talking about Holmes — her case is closed, and she’s in federal prison — but her con-artistry has fascinated the media (myself included) for the last decade.
In fact, as Shultz says in an interview with The San Francisco Standard, “the only reason we’re talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants us to be talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now.”
But the cautionary tale of Theranos takes on a new significance as we enter the peak of the AI era, when companies that have never turned a profit are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations.
“I think the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over. Elizabeth took that model and scaled it to $100 million,” Shultz told SF Standard.
His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable investor and board member himself.
“I believe that what [Holmes] did was raise the biggest angel round of funding of all time, but even at the smaller levels, I think investors need to recognize that when they put that type of money in someone’s hands, they are giving them tremendous power,” he added.
Theranos’ funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families, rather than venture firms. Theranos did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing concerns about revealing trade secrets, which warded off many top venture capitalists in Silicon Valley.
At the time Theranos’ fraud was uncovered, it was seen as a shrill wake-up call for investors that they need to prioritize due diligence. But in the AI era, Shultz worries that investors may forget these lessons.
“A huge danger with AI is that I think it is really hard to do due diligence on it,” he said. “It’s really hard to tell the difference between what is something truly unique and new versus like, a ChatGPT wrapper… If you want to deceive people, I think this is a great opportunity to go deceive people.”
The first question posed by “You Can See Everything” lies in the premise of the movie itself. Why would a mother of two young children choose to invite a film crew to follow her final days with her family before surrendering to serve a prison sentence of over 11 years? The film poses questions that seem inscrutable, but this one seems pretty clear. She wants people to pity her, because this pity could be more useful for her future endeavors than hate or mockery.
In the film, we see Holmes and her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, working on Haemanthus, a diagnostics company that they call “Theranos 2.0,” which has reportedly raised about $20 million in funding.
“You Can See Everything” doesn’t make Holmes look good, but it also glosses over the more heinous crimes of Theranos, like giving dangerously faulty medical information to real patients, or even its targeted harassment of Shultz himself when he was attempting to sound the alarm about his former employer. In the cultural zeitgeist, Holmes remains more of a joke than a persona non grata.
“I have this feeling of unease about what might come next,” Shultz said. “She’s certainly preparing and beginning her second act, and I don’t know exactly where it’s going to go.”
